correlation_matrix.title: Correlation with survival and among numeric features

key_findings: Overall survival rate was 38% (339 of 888 passengers).
Women survived at 74%, men at 19% — a 55% gap.
1st-class passengers survived at 62%, vs 24% for 3rd class.
The strongest pattern: 1st-class women survived at 97%; 3rd-class men at 14%.
Families of 2–4 survived better than singles or very large families — a non-linear effect.
Fare correlates positively with survival (+0.26), mostly as a proxy for class.

pipeline_sections.title: 1. Loading
pipeline_sections.summary: Pull the dataset once and persist it as a CSV so the rest of the pipeline behaves like real-world data.

steps.title: Load Titanic and cache a raw CSV
steps.why: Seaborn gives us a clean Python entry point, but real datasets arrive as files. Writing the raw CSV once means every later step reads from disk, which matches how you'd work with any real dataset.

pipeline_sections.title: 2. Cleaning
pipeline_sections.summary: Remove redundant columns, fill missing values with appropriate strategies, and filter out extreme outliers.

steps.title: Drop redundant columns
steps.why: `class` duplicates `pclass`, `alive` duplicates `survived`, `embark_town` duplicates `embarked`, and `adult_male` is derivable from `sex` + `age`. Carrying duplicates risks subtle bugs in groupby and correlation.

steps.title: Fill missing `embarked` with the mode
steps.why: Only 2 rows have missing `embarked`. The mode ('S', Southampton) is by far the most common port, so single-value imputation is safe.

steps.title: Fill missing `deck` with 'Unknown'
steps.why: 77% of `deck` is missing — too sparse to impute realistically. An explicit 'Unknown' bucket keeps the column usable in charts and groupby (rows aren't silently dropped).

steps.title: Impute missing `age` by (pclass, sex) median
steps.why: A global median erases information — a 1st-class woman has a very different age profile than a 3rd-class man. Group-wise medians via `groupby().transform()` preserve that signal.
steps.result: 177 missing ages filled using the median of each (class, sex) group.

steps.title: Drop fare outliers (> $300)
steps.why: Three passengers paid $512 — over 10× the median fare. They distort the fare distribution and dominate correlations. A simple boolean mask removes them.

pipeline_sections.title: 3. Feature engineering
pipeline_sections.summary: Derive new columns that capture relationships the raw data only hints at.

steps.title: `family_size` + boolean flags
steps.why: Spouses/siblings and parents/children live in separate columns. Combining them (+1 for the passenger) creates a single number with a non-linear effect on survival. We also derive two convenience booleans for filtering and modeling.

steps.title: `age_group` via `pd.cut` (fixed bins)
steps.why: Continuous age is hard to compare across cohorts. `pd.cut` bins by fixed thresholds — useful when the boundaries (child/teen/adult/senior) are conceptually meaningful, not just statistically equal-sized.
steps.code:
df['age_group'] = pd.cut(
    df['age'],
    bins=[0, 12, 17, 59, np.inf],
    labels=['Child', 'Teen', 'Adult', 'Senior'],
)

steps.title: `fare_per_person` = fare / family_size
steps.why: A $200 ticket for a family of 5 is very different from a $200 solo fare. Per-person fare is often the cleaner signal for class.
steps.code:
df['fare_per_person'] = np.where(
    df['family_size'] > 0,
    df['fare'] / df['family_size'],
    df['fare'],
)
steps.result: Per-person fares range from $0 to ~$73 (after outlier filter).

steps.title: `fare_tier` via `pd.qcut` (equal-count bins)
steps.why: Where `pd.cut` uses fixed thresholds, `pd.qcut` makes 4 buckets of equal size — useful when you want a 'low/mid/high/premium' split that's robust to outliers and skew.

steps.title: `cabin_known` from `deck`
steps.why: Whether the cabin was *recorded* is itself signal — it correlates with class (1st-class records are more complete). A simple comparison turns the 'Unknown' bucket into a binary feature.
steps.result: 200 passengers have a known cabin, 688 don't.

pipeline_sections.title: 4. Encoding & normalization
pipeline_sections.summary: Convert categoricals to numeric encodings and put continuous features on a comparable scale — the inputs most ML models expect.

steps.title: Binary encode `sex` → `is_female`
steps.why: A boolean comparison cast to int gives a single 0/1 column that can enter correlation matrices and regressions directly. Sex turns out to be the single strongest predictor of survival.

steps.title: One-hot encode `embarked` via `pd.get_dummies`
steps.why: Ports C / Q / S have no natural ordering, so an ordinal encoding would lie. One-hot encoding splits the column into 3 mutually-exclusive binary columns — the right shape for any linear model.
steps.code:
embarked_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df['embarked'], prefix='emb').astype(int)
df = pd.concat([df, embarked_dummies], axis=1)
steps.result: Adds emb_C, emb_Q, emb_S (one column per port).

steps.title: Log-transform `fare` → `log_fare`
steps.why: Fare is heavily right-skewed: most people paid under $50, a few paid hundreds. `np.log1p` (= log(1+x)) compresses the long tail while gracefully handling fare = $0 (which plain `log` can't).
steps.result: Distribution becomes roughly bell-shaped, friendlier to most models.

steps.title: Z-score normalize age and fare
steps.why: Different features live on different scales — age (0-80) and fare ($0-$300) aren't comparable. Subtracting the mean and dividing by the std gives both a mean of 0 and an std of 1, so distance-based methods (KNN, PCA, gradient descent) treat them fairly.
steps.code:
df['age_z']  = (df['age']  - df['age'].mean())  / df['age'].std()
df['fare_z'] = (df['fare'] - df['fare'].mean()) / df['fare'].std()
steps.result: Both columns now centered at 0 with unit std.

pipeline_sections.title: 5. Analysis
pipeline_sections.summary: The three pandas patterns that produce every number in the dashboard.

steps.title: Groupby + agg for survival rates
steps.why: Survival is encoded as 0/1, so the mean of `survived` is literally the survival rate. One groupby gives you both the count (`n`) and the rate at once.

steps.title: Crosstab for two-dimensional rates
steps.why: Single-variable comparisons can be confounded — class survival differs partly because women cluster in 1st class. A `sex × class` crosstab disentangles the two.
steps.result: 1st-class women: 97%; 3rd-class men: 14%. The strongest pattern in the dataset.

steps.title: Correlation matrix
steps.why: For numeric features, `.corr()` quickly reveals which are linearly related — both to the target (survival) and to each other (potential redundancy).
steps.result: Fare correlates +0.26 with survival; family_size correlates +0.89 with sibsp (as expected — they overlap).
